newsitem.title: GERMANY: Early German tax deal unlikely - SPD expert.
newsitem.headline: Early German tax deal unlikely - SPD expert.

text.p: Germany's tax reform project will probably end up in parliament's conflict-resolution process rather than being decided at the negotiating table, a leader from the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said on Wednesday.
Speaking a day after the coalition and SPD failed to make any breakthroughs at tax talks, Hamburg mayor Henning Voscherau said time was running short to reach a compromise.
"These negotiations...will be caught up and even overtaken by the legislative process," Voscherau, one of the SPD's top tax negotiators, told North German Radio.

The two sides agreed to meet again for further talks next Wednesday to discuss Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plan to cut 30 billion marks ($17 billion) in taxes to boost investment and cut high German unemployment.
But government leaders vowed to press on with getting legislation through the Bundestag lower house before the summer break -- whether or not the talks with the SPD succeed.
The SPD has said it wants the government to agree on a cut of two percentage points in labour insurance charges from July to give the German jobs market a boost.

The coalition agreed to make a one-point cut -- but only if the SPD gives its full backing to its tax plans. Waigel also says the contributions cuts should go hand-in-hand with reforms to state pensions, health and jobless schemes.
Asked whether that meant that the tax reforms would end up in parliament's mediation process, Voscherau said: "That is likely."

"We must try to pull the cart out of the mud, because it is clear that it is stuck ever deeper into the mud," he told the radio. "But we will not do that at the expense of giving up our own convictions."
The SPD can block tax laws in the Bundesrat upper house of parliament, where Voscherau is a member.
Stalemate would make the tax issue a key campaign issue in a series of regional elections leading up to a general election in autumn 1998. Polls will be held in Hamburg in September.
Other regional SPD chiefs weighed in to the tax debate, warning that Waigel would have no chance of getting such a big net tax cut through the Bundesrat.
Hans Eichel, premier of the mid-German state of Hesse, said it was "completely out of the question" for Waigel to cut taxes.
"Otherwise we will completely miss the Maastricht criteria," Eichel told Deutsche Welle radio.
The Maastricht treaty governing European monetary union sets a budget deficit limit of three percent of gross domestic product -- a figure Waigel is straining to meet this year.

Manfred Stolpe, SPD premier in Brandenburg, said Waigel's tax cuts would cost his eastern German state 400 million marks a year. "We don't know how we could cope with that. It's the same for the other states," he told InfoRadio Berlin.
Waigel said on Tuesday he was prepared to go some way towards meeting the concerns of regional leaders by negotiating on the basis of a "30 billion minus x" formula.
But he remains under pressure to achieve a big net tax cut from junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), who say a revenue-neutral tax reform would not be worth the effort.
The FDP's chief tax negotiator Hermann Otto Solms said the coalition was still ready to reach a quick tax deal with the SPD, but said Tuesday's talks were "disappointing overall".
"We are not clinging to numbers, but on the other hand it must be clear that the coalition is not retreating from its reform goals," he told reporters.
($ = 1.726 German Marks)
